text.en: Look around you. Which things or people make you laugh? In this poem by Natalie Joan, a very strange man walks down the street, and everything he does is upside down. Let us see how nonsense can be great fun.

You look around for things or people that make you laugh, write them in bubbles and share your reasons with your classmates and teacher.
One day a funny man comes walking down the street. He wears a shoe on his head and hats on his feet. He raises the shoe to the poet and smiles, and he is polite, but the poet has never seen such a funny sounding sight. The man offers a rose to Your Highness, but takes out a currant bun and holds it to the poet's nose. The poet staggers back against the wall and says she never saw a rose with such a funny looking smell. He sings a song and sits on the ground, and the poet says no one has ever heard such a funny feeling sound. The poet asks him why he wears two hats on his feet. In reply he turns the other way about and hops home on his head.
In the true or false exercise, these are true: the poet says she had never heard such an amusing song, the funny man wore two hats on his feet, he hopped home on his head, and he smiled at the poet. It is false that he was ill-mannered, since his manners were polite, and false that he gave her a real rose, since he held out a currant bun. A currant is a small seedless raisin, and staggered means moved unsteadily. The tone of the poem is humorous, because the man does silly things such as wearing a shoe on his head. The poem has a sing-song rhythm which gives it a musical, playful quality. The word funny is repeated again and again to stress how very odd and amusing everything is. The vivid imagery creates a humorous and nonsensical scene.
The poet mixes up the senses on purpose. A sound that you can see, a smell that looks and a sound that you feel are nonsense phrases, which is what makes the poem funny. Sounding sight and hopped home are alliteration, because words begin with the same sound. Sometimes poets change the usual order of words, called inversion, to keep the rhythm. For example, But never had I seen before such a funny sounding sight can be set in the usual order as I had never seen such a funny sounding sight before. The funny man addresses the poet as Your Highness to be playful and polite, as if she were royalty. Allow me to present is a polite request. When the poet says Well! she is surprised because a bun was held out as a rose. The poet calls him my friend because she is not angry but amused. His reaction to her question tells us he is cheerful and eccentric, and the last line leaves readers feeling cheerful.
What appeals to you about the funny man? Perhaps his politeness, his cheerfulness or his imagination. His unusual actions make the mood light and silly. Another title could be The Upside-Down Man, because he wears things in the wrong place and goes home on his head. The poet includes the man's and her own words to make the poem lively, like a little conversation, and she wishes to show how nonsense and laughter can bring joy. In real life, clowns, mimes, street performers and comedians do silly things for fun and entertainment.
A phrasal verb is a verb with a preposition or adverb that together work as a single unit, such as walking down. The meaning is often different from the single words, and the same verb with different words gives different meanings. The take group: take up means to begin to study, practise or do something. Take after means to resemble a family member. Take in means to understand or comprehend. Take over means to assume control or responsibility. Take off means to become successful or popular quickly. The sentence blanks are: new technology will take over traditional methods; I tried hard to take in what the writer wanted to say; Arjun decided to take up painting; the smartphone quickly took off in the market; Sheela takes after her father. Other examples are look after, which means take care of, and look up, run away, put off, break down and call off. Make your own sentences with five phrasal verbs. The words walking, staggered and hopped show different ways of moving. In order of pace, walk is slow, jog is faster, run is faster still and sprint is the fastest.
For the speaking task you read a joke about a man who asks God how long a million years is. God says it is a minute, and a million rupees is less than a rupee, so the man asks for a rupee and God says wait a minute. Tell it using a respectful voice for the man, a deep voice for God and an even voice for the narrator, then make up your own joke. A limerick is a funny five-line verse, and all limericks follow the rhyme scheme AABBA, as in Edward Lear's example about an old man with a beard. Write your own: line one introduces a person or place, lines two to four tell a silly story, and line five ends the joke.

why.en: Take after means resemble a family member; take over means assume control or responsibility.

text.en: Use each in a sentence.

why.en: Sheela takes after her father. The new manager took over the work.

problem.en: Write the rhyme scheme of a limerick.

text.en: Count the lines.
Mark the rhymes.

why.en: Lines 1, 2 and 5 rhyme and lines 3 and 4 rhyme: AABBA.

prompt.en: Describe the funny man and explain why the poem is funny.

requiredIdeas.en: He wears a shoe on his head and hats on his feet.
He gives a currant bun instead of a rose and sings a strange song.
He hops home on his head.
The poet mixes up the senses and uses repetition and a sing-song rhythm.

commonMisconceptions.en: The poem is serious in tone.

points.en: A Funny Man is a humorous nonsense poem by Natalie Joan.
The funny man wears a shoe on his head and hats on his feet, and hops home on his head.
Mixed senses, repetition of funny, alliteration and inversion add fun.
Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a preposition or adverb to make a new meaning.
A limerick has five lines with the rhyme scheme AABBA.
